claims.text: Adding a controlled dispersion of nanoscale stable oxide particles to a refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its radiation tolerance.
The oxide dispersion will preserve the refractory high-entropy alloy's mechanical integrity.
The initial refractory high-entropy alloy has a coarse, nearly homogeneous matrix.
The initial alloy has limited intrinsic defect-sink capability under irradiation.
Controlled oxidation or reactive alloying can create a uniform nanodispersion of stable oxide particles in the alloy matrix.
High-flux helium-ion irradiation at 600–1000 °C provides a simulation of fusion plasma-facing conditions.
The intervention will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale stable oxide particles in both the grain boundaries and matrix.
Nanoscale oxide particles act as sinks for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Nanoscale oxide particles act as sinks for helium bubbles.
Defect and helium-bubble sink activity will reduce irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Reduced defect accumulation will mitigate irradiation-induced embrittlement while preserving the load-bearing matrix.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will have a lower irradiation-induced defect density.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will retain or improve yield strength.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will retain or improve ductility.
The beneficial effect requires oxide particles to be appropriately sized and well distributed.
Excessive oxide content may cause phase segregation or embrittlement.
Insufficient oxide dispersion may provide too few defect sinks to improve radiation tolerance.
Direct experimental evidence for oxide-dispersion-enhanced radiation tolerance in refractory high-entropy alloys under fusion-relevant conditions is currently lacking.
